content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach to apply the principle of independent causal mechanism (ICM) for causal discovery of bivariate systems in a quantitative manner. The variation-based cause effect identification (VCEI) approach artificially generates changes in the marginal of one covariate and assesses the difference in the conditional distributions as a result of the artificially-generated changes. The proposed changes in the marginals are re-weighting the empirical marginal distribution and the resulting conditional distribution changes are assessed by computing the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between trained predictive models trained on the original marginal versus the tweaked marginal. Finding the reweighted empirical distribution is framed as an optimization problem that maximizes the MMD between the original empirical distribution and the reweighted empirical distribution. VCEI is also experimentally validated with other causal discovery approaches e.g. ANM-based, ICGI on synthetic and real-world data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper proposes a quantifiable way of using ICM for causal discovery. Because of the discrepancy measure used, it seems that VCEI can be applied to a wide variety of data spaces. I count the discussion of the practical considerations as a strength too. 

While the VCEI approach appears sound, I have a few concerns: 
1) Empirical results: The only way of validating the VCEI approach here seemed to be using empirical results. While the authors are upfront about the fact that the performance isn't the best, it is important to note that there are datasets on which every other method performed much better than VCEI.  
2) This paper would be much stronger if there were some theoretical validation of VCEI. As the authors point out, "..identifiability of ICM-based frameworks increase with increasing non-linearity of the functional form, smaller noise effects..". It would strengthen the paper to show these for VCEI analytically. Is there even any theoretical framework to compare VCEi with other ICM-based methods?  
3) Scalability while discussed already in the paper, is another issue to make this practical. Perhaps some empirical effect of scalability would add more value to the paper?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper reads well and clear except some places where notation is used without explanation. (e.g. 3.2 - Train[.] is used for the first time without much explanation). While the use of MMD metrics in causal discovery has been done before, using it in a quantifiable ICM-based approach is novel and original.
content.summary_of_the_review: The lack of any striking empirical performance and absence of any theoretical validation of VCEI are major points to recommend rejection. I am happy to be corrected if I have misunderstood some results.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on the bivariate causal discovery problem. It claims that the proposed method relies on the independence of cause and mechansim (ICM). There are two steps of the methods. First, it introduces variations to the potential cause mechanism. Second, it estimates two models for both causal and reverse causal direction, of which one is trained on orginal data and another is trained on the data with the introduced variation. Then it computes the discrepancy of the distributions of the predicted results with the two models for each direction. Finally, it concludes the causal direction with the smaller discrepancy. Both steps use MMD for maximizing variations and compute the discrepancy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
(+) The article starts by introducing the context and idea with a nice illustration figure.
(+) The procedure of step 1 is well illustrated. It formulates the problem in a clear way and solves it as a convex optimization problem.
(+) It includes the limitations in a transparent way, which shows that the task is difficult. 

My main concerns are about the clarification and justification of the proposed method, which is listed in __Clarification__. Moreover, given the comparison with the other methods mentioned in the related work and the limitations of the proposed method, the method has limited novelty, significance, and interests, though the use of MMD and ICM brings certain interests. 

I will make it clear as the actionable feedback in the following. 

The significance and the novelty from the method perspective:

(i) The essential elements of the method are 1) introducing variations to $p_x$, 2) fitting models with the data from $p_{x,y}$ and from $p_{x,y}^{\alpha}$; 3) measuring the discrepancy of the predictive distirbution of $p_y$. 
From the perspective of implementing ICM principle, maybe try to motivate why would the framework be considered as significant or novel compared with the others? 

(ii) Sec. 3.1 introduce a way to add variations but it is not clear how it is necessary to add in this way compared with the naive ways. More can be seen in the third point of the Clarification part. Except that, I do find that the formulation and solution of the problem in Sec. 3.1 is interesting. But it seems that (9-13) are the direct implication and derivation of (Park & Boyd 2017). Thus, it may have limited novelty.


The significance from the empirical performance/benefits perspective:

(iii) if the significance is from empirical performance, then the paper should include more in the experiment section and explain more about where and how the proposed method is better than the related works.
Especially, the current experiment section only shows the performance from one aspect. Then, maybe try to motivate why would the proposed method be considered as significantly better than the others in certain aspects? And why would such aspects be considered as important and significant in the field? Furthermore, it is also necessary to support the claims with experiments
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
(-) The proposed method is claimed to be a practical realization of the ICM principle. However, it is not clear enough how the method is corresponding to the ICM principle. Especially, the ICM introduced in Sec. 2 states that in the causal direction $p_{y|x}$ is independent of $p_x$; whereas, the proposed method consists of two steps and how the two steps are practicing the ICM principle and explicitly/implicitly measuring the ICM principle? For example, how (14) is quantifying the impact of the introduced variations in the cause (distribution)? The ICM principle is about the conditional and the marginal while (14) is about the discrepancy of marginals, which is not straightforward to see how.

(-) A following-up point is about identifiability. Without elaborating on the previous point, it is not clear to see how the identifiability with the proposed method can inherit from the ICM principle. Please also elaborate on this point: how the identifiability with the ICM principle entails the identifiability with the proposed method. 

(-) Step 1 in Sec. 3 is motivated by the non-negligible variation. It lacks a justification for how the proposed method is dealing with the issue and guarantees non-negligible variation. Because to be maximal is not necessary to be non-negligible. Why is it reasonable to compute the maximal variation and use it for implementing the ICM principle? The non-negligible variation is with respect to measuring the causal direction. So maybe first make it clear what is non-negligible, how to measure such property, and then how to enforce and guarantee it. 


(-) Based on the description and the algorithm, it is not clear how to learn the predictive functions, especially the one with $\hat{f}^{\alpha}_{y|x}$.


(-) In Sec. 3.2 the are typos at "y->y"
content.summary_of_the_review: The article provides a method, which applies the ICM principle for causal discovery. My main concerns are about the clarification and the lack of significance and technical novelty.  It requires a justification of the proposed method. And it is not clear how the proposed method is corresponding to the ICM principle and how identifiability is guaranteed

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach to the classic problem of cause-effect identification, i.e., given a pair of dependent random variables, distinguishing which is the cause and which is the effect. The proposal is an instantiation of the principle of independence of cause and mechanism, according to which, in the underlying causal relationship, the distribution of the cause and the cause-effect mechanism are functionally independent. The paper proposes to exploit this principle by imposing artificial variations to both marginal distributions, and then assessing how these variations impact the corresponding conditionals of the other variable, choosing as the causal relationship the one in which this impact is lower. To implement this approach, the authors use several technical tools, namely, the kernel-based maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to assess how different two sets of samples are. The experimental results show that the proposed method performs well (though not beating the state of the art), with its main advantage being, arguably, that the use of kernel-based MMD encapsulates the method from the particular type of data that is being studied, as long as an adequate kernel can be defined.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The proposed method is an interesting instantiation of the principle of independence of cause and mechanism, which is the core idea that underlies much of causal discovery, namely in the bivariate case addressed in this paper. The main strength of the paper is, in my opinion, the use of the kernel-based MMD, which encapsulates the method from the particular type of data that is being studied, as long as an adequate kernel can be defined. 

The paper has several weaknesses, both at the superficial and conceptual levels. It is not very well written, with several wrong, or at least unsupported, statements. For example, In the third paragraph, the authors claim that they "exploit a barely explored interpretation of this principle, namely that these sub-mechanisms do not influence each other" (where the principle referred to is that of independence of cause and mechanism), which is clearly not true. Most instantiations of this principle can be obviously interpreted precisely as ways of assessing how independent the cause-effect mechanism is from the cause (or the distribution thereof). 

In Section 3.1, the authors introduce a formulation (Problem 1 and its optimization form in (6), (7), (8)) and adopt an algorithm to obtain the sample weighting that maximizes the MMD with respect to the original distribution. The authors seem to be unaware of the following well known fact from optimization: a concave function achieves its minimum over a compact convex set at an extreme point of that set. Since the constraint set (in (7)-(8)) is just the simplex, which is compact and convex, the solution is simply an atom (i.e., one of the components of $\alpha$ equal to 1 and all the others equal to zero). Finding which data point should have the weight one can simply be obtained by maximizing (5) with respect to all such $N$ possible choices. The reformulation in (9)-(13) and the corresponding algorithm to solve it are thus useless. The authors eventually find out that the solutions are of this nature (in Section 3.3), but fail to trace back this fact to the nature of problem (6)-(8), and try to tackle what they see as a drawback by imposing an additional constraint in the problem (9)-(13). 

The scaling concern that the authors mention in the second paragraph of Section 3.3 is not only related to the lifting that underlies the reformulation (9)-(13); in fact, it is already present in (5), since computing the Gram matrix has quadratic cost in the number of points.

Finally, the authors eventually recognize (in the first paragraph of Section 3.3) that it is not clear that it makes sense to look for the most discrepant distribution w.r.t. the original one, and that other "more appealing" solutions may be preferred. Arguably, this invalidates most of the work described in Section 3.1, rendering it somewhat useless. The main reasoning flaw seems to be the unjustified jump (made in Section 3.1) from looking simply for a "non-negligible variation" to looking for the most discrepant variation, as formulated in Problem 1.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written but has a few writing issues. For example, I urge the authors to read about the difference between \citep and \citet and their usage. 

For the reasons pointed out in the previous review section (Strength And Weaknesses), the paper has some flaws that affect its overall quality. 

The method is novel, but its rationale is not fully well supported, as argued in the previous review section.

The method is not too difficult to reproduce, since the algorithms are rather straightforward and the datasets used are public.
content.summary_of_the_review: A reasonably good idea (variation-based cause-effect identification), but poorly instantiated and with several flaws.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides a new method of identifying a causal direction in the bivariate setting. The proposed method leverages the ICM principle explicitly.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
###  Strength
1. This paper is very well and clearly written.
2. The proposed method is straightforward and easy to understand.
3. An introduction contains an insightful overview of the contribution.

### Weakness
1. I think the contribution compared to existing methods can be more explicitly written. How do existing works have tackled? What’s the novelty of the proposed method compared to other works? I am somewhat surprised by this paper because the proposed method is quite a simple and good solution for the important bivariate causal discovery problem.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I will put some issues and questions in this section.

### Suggestions
1. When you write “Problem 1” in Section 3.1., For consistency, I think it’s good to have “Problem 2” in Section 3.2.
2. There is a typo in the last line of Algo. 1.
3. As written as a weakness of the paper, I think the contribution should be more explicitly written. In its current shape, it’s hard to see what’s the competitive advantage or novelty of this paper compared to many other papers tackling the same problem.

### Questions.
1. Is $\hat{f}$ a predictive model or an empirical conditional distribution? If it’s a predictive model, how can one measure the MMD to the prediction model? I thought only a distribution could be an input of the MMD.
2. Is there an assumption that the true data-generating process is either X→Y or Y → X?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the paper is written clearly, and the quality is good. I think that the paper can be improved by explicitly highlighting its contributions compared to existing works tackling the same problem. I also would like to see how questions and suggestions will be handled because these are the main concerns when I read the paper.

content.title: Variation-based Cause Effect Identification
content.TL;DR: A framework for causal discovery in bivariate systems based on realization of the independence of causal mechanisms postulate using convex-optimization
content.abstract: Mining genuine mechanisms underlying the complex data generation process in real-world systems is a fundamental step in promoting interpretability of (and thus trust in) data-driven models. Therefore, we propose a variation-based cause effect \underline{i}dentification (VCEI) framework for causal discovery in bivariate systems from a single observational setting. Our framework relies on the principle of independence of cause and mechanism (ICM) under the assumption of an existing acyclic causal link, and offers a practical realization of this principle. Principally, we artificially construct two settings in which the marginal distributions of one covariate, claimed to be the cause, are guaranteed to have non-negligible variations. This is achieved by re-weighting samples of the marginal so that the resultant distribution is notably distinct from this marginal according to some discrepancy measure. In the causal direction, such variations are expected to have no impact on the effect generation mechanism. Therefore, quantifying the impact of these variations on the conditionals reveals the genuine causal direction. Moreover, we formulate our approach in the kernel-based maximum mean discrepancy, lifting all constraints on the data types of cause and effect covariates, and rendering such artificial interventions a convex optimization problem. We provide a series of experiments on real and synthetic data showing that VCEI is, in principle, competitive to other cause effect identification frameworks.
